Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The blotter lists every order for the account newest first, rejections included, with a badge per status carrying the word as well as the colour. \\ * An order sitting at NEW is shown as still working and is brought up to date by a bounded re-read. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Render the order table from the order-history endpoint with formatted dates and values. \\  \\ Badge NEW, FILLED, REJECTED and CANCELLED, carrying the word as well as the colour, because roughly one man in twelve cannot separate red from green. \\  \\ Re-read order history on a bounded interval while anything is at NEW, offer a refresh the user can press, and stop when nothing is working. \\  \\ Never re-post the order: the same idempotency key returns a conflict and a new key places a second order. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # order history renders newest first including rejections \\ # an order at NEW is shown as still working \\ # the re-read stops when nothing is at NEW \\ # empty history is handled gracefully \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A blotter that hides rejected orders is worse than no blotter: the rejection is the record that the desk tried and was refused. \\ * An interval that never stops is a request every couple of seconds for as long as the tab is open, which is a load test you did not mean to run.

Summary: Playwright: Sign In and Place an Order
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Two Playwright journeys run against the real running stack: signing in and placing an order. \\ * Each journey stands on its own, in its own process, leaving nothing behind that another journey needs. \\ * Every address and credential is read from the environment under the declared names. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Configure Playwright as soon as sign-in works, because the journeys need the whole stack up. \\  \\ Cover the guard redirect, a refused sign-in, a successful sign-in and arriving where you were going. \\  \\ Cover the read-only account, a rejection before submission, and a placed order with whatever status came back. \\  \\ Accept NEW, FILLED or REJECTED on a placed order; a spec that asserts FILLED fails the week the executor is switched on. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Two journeys is the assessed set for this cohort. A third over the blotter is worth writing if the time is there and is declared in manifest.env. \\ * Shared state on your side is what breaks isolation: a token stashed in a module variable, or an order one spec placed that the next expects.

Summary: Secret-Free Production Bundle
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The production build contains no API key, no signing secret and no market-data host. \\ * The application never calls the Fauxnance API; prices reach the browser through a service of yours that holds the key server-side. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Build the production bundle and search it for key and secret patterns, and for the market-data host. \\  \\ Confirm nothing under a different name carries the literal value of your key or signing secret. \\  \\ Treat a key that reached a bundle as published: revoke it rather than deleting the line. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * There is no private part of a front-end build. Minification is not obfuscation, and a source map is the source back again. \\ * This check remains mandatory for this cohort.

Summary: Extension Services (Four Mandatory)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * All four extensions are built and integrated end to end, in the dependency order Customer Preferences, then Customer Notifications, then Watchlists and Price Alerts, with Portfolio and P&L built in parallel. \\ * Each is a separate service that verifies the platform JWT itself and authorises on its own routes, and each runs on live data at the demonstration. \\ * One combined OWASP security review covers all four with its findings addressed, and an architecture decision log is committed. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * All four extensions are mandatory for this cohort. They are not alternatives. Trade Advice and Signals and Automated Strategy Execution are stretch goals, available only once all four services pass the harness. \\ * Three of the four have no contract: their APIs are yours to design, written as OpenAPI before the controller and reviewed by an instructor on day one. Portfolio and P&L is bound by contracts/portfolio-api.yaml. \\ * Nothing is scaffolded here because there is nothing to scaffold until you have designed it. The folder holds the four briefs, the two documents and the harness. \\ * Process is assessed alongside product. A team that ships four running services with no backlog, no decision log and a security review written on the Thursday evening scores below a team that ships less and can show how it was decided. \\ * This is the last sprint in which the platform is assessed. The demonstration happens at the end of this week against a running stack, and the cloud week that follows is assessed on the deployment alone. \\ * Definition of done includes sprint-10-extension-service/scripts/check.sh, and scripts/check.sh --live once the stack is up. \\ * Security focus: the full OWASP Top Ten across four services, starting with the access-control row, because all four hold data belonging to one customer and reachable with a token belonging to another.

Summary: Day One: Read the Briefs, Confirm Scope, Write the Backlog
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Every member has read all four briefs, and the scope is confirmed with an instructor on the Monday. \\ * A backlog with acceptance criteria covers all four services before any code is written. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read all four catalogue briefs as a team, not one each. \\  \\ Bring to the instructor what you intend to build by Friday, what you have decided not to build, and the APIs you propose to expose for the three services that have no contract. \\  \\ Write the backlog for all four services, in whatever tracker the team has been using, before writing code. \\  \\ Plan the work by the order of the chain rather than one person per service: four people starting four services on Monday morning produces three of them blocked by lunchtime. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Scope confirmed on day one is an acceptance criterion, not a courtesy. \\ * A backlog assembled on Friday morning from the commits is visible as one.

Summary: Agree the Two Integration Seams
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The route notifications calls on preferences, and the route watchlists calls on notifications, are written down on the Monday with their response shapes and their behaviour when no preference has been set. \\ * How a service authenticates to a service is decided and recorded, rather than reusing a customer token. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Agree both seams before either side builds against a guess. \\  \\ Decide how a service calls a service, given that neither caller holds a customer's token and reusing one would turn a fifteen-minute credential into a permanent one. \\  \\ Decide what each caller does when the service it depends on does not answer, and record the choice. \\  \\ Give every consumer an explicit group identifier, listed in its README and shared with no other service. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A route that another service calls, reachable by a customer with a customer's token, is an access-control failure the Sprint 8 review had no equivalent of.

Summary: Customer Preferences and Personalisation
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A preference record per customer holds at least a default account and an alert channel with its contact detail, and it survives a restart of the service. \\ * The stored default is applied at the customer's next sign-in in the Angular application. \\ * A resolution route exists for the notification path to call, and it is not reachable by a customer with a customer's token under the same rules. \\ * Every read and write is scoped to the account in the verified token. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Design the API, write it as OpenAPI before the controller, and bring it to an instructor on day one. \\  \\ Build the service on its own port, in its own folder under services/, with its own Dockerfile, compose entry and README. \\  \\ Verify the platform JWT in this service on every route and compare the account claim against the account being addressed. \\  \\ Separate the internal resolution path from the customer path, or put it behind a service credential, and say which you chose. \\  \\ Decide what is stored here and what is referenced, given that an email address and a telephone number are personal data that may already exist elsewhere on the platform. \\  \\ Decide what the platform does when no preference has been set, and what a caller does when this service does not answer. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # preferences are saved and read back \\ # preferences survive a restart of the service \\ # another account's preferences are refused rather than returned empty \\ # the stored default is applied at next sign-in \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Build this one first. Notifications cannot route a message without a channel, and watchlists reaches the same preference one step further along the chain. \\ * A route that answers with a plausible shape before its persistence is finished unblocks the rest of the team on Monday afternoon. \\ * Availability matters more than feature surface here: another service calls this one synchronously on the path that decides whether a customer hears about their own trade.

Summary: Customer Notifications
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The service consumes trade-events in a group of its own and handles the filled, rejected and cancelled outcomes. \\ * The channel is resolved from Customer Preferences on every send rather than from a constant, and the resolved channel is recorded on the notification. \\ * A replayed event produces no second message, and notification history is readable only by the owning account. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Design the API, write it as OpenAPI before the controller, and bring it to an instructor on day one. \\  \\ Build the service on its own port with its own folder, Dockerfile, compose entry and README, verifying the platform JWT itself. \\  \\ Commit the offset once the notification is durably recorded for delivery, not once an external provider has confirmed, and track queued, sent and failed separately. \\  \\ Key idempotency on the event identifier so that a second delivery is a no-op. \\  \\ Deliver on at least one channel; a logging stub is acceptable for a channel you cannot provision, provided the routing decision is real and the resolved channel is recorded. \\  \\ Expose the route watchlists calls to have an alert delivered, and decide how a service authenticates to it. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a filled order produces a notification \\ # a rejected order produces a notification \\ # the channel comes from Customer Preferences and changing the preference changes the channel used \\ # a replayed event does not send a second message \\ # notification history is refused to an account that does not own it \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Do not start this before preferences has a route that answers. Hardcoding a channel is the one shortcut this service does not have, because the criterion is delivery on the channel preferences holds. \\ * A rejection is as newsworthy as a fill: a customer who only hears about successes has no idea their order failed. \\ * A webhook target or channel destination a customer can set, and the service then posts to, is a server-side request forgery.

Summary: Watchlists and Price Alerts
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The service consumes market-data in a group of its own, and a customer can create a watchlist, add instruments and see a live price beside each entry. \\ * A price alert has a threshold and a direction, is evaluated against the stream, and a crossed threshold is delivered through Customer Notifications on the channel the customer configured. \\ * Alert state is visible to the customer, and alerts are capped per account. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Design the API, write it as OpenAPI before the controller, and bring it to an instructor on day one. \\  \\ Build the service on its own port with its own folder, Dockerfile, compose entry and README, verifying the platform JWT itself. \\  \\ Consume market-data only. Do not consume orders or trade-events; neither says anything about what a customer is curious about. \\  \\ Index the per-quote lookup, because every quote for every symbol arrives here and the service has to decide per message whether any customer cares. \\  \\ Define what crossed means and what happens next: deactivate, wait for a reset, or fire on every quote past the level, and record why. \\  \\ Hand a triggered alert to notifications rather than resolving a channel here, and decide what happens when notifications does not answer. \\  \\ Cap alerts per account so that an unbounded creation route cannot turn your own consumer into the thing that takes the service down. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # a watchlist is created and scoped to the authenticated account \\ # an instrument is added and shows a live price \\ # a quote crossing a threshold triggers the alert \\ # a quote short of the threshold does not trigger it \\ # the alert is delivered through notifications rather than to a log \\ # alert creation is capped per account \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Build this last of the three in the chain. An alert written only to a log has not met the criterion. \\ * A watchlist entry is not a position: a customer must be able to watch something they have never traded. \\ * Firing on every quote past the level sends a customer forty messages in a minute, through a service somebody else on your team is responsible for.

Summary: Portfolio and P&L
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The service implements contracts/portfolio-api.yaml: the three routes and the health check, with the exact field names and the error catalogue the contract fixes. \\ * Positions are priced from live Fauxnance quotes, batched and cached, and every priced figure carries when it was observed and whether it is stale. \\ * Where pricing is unavailable for every held instrument the service answers with the documented service-unavailable code; where it is unavailable for some, the response is partial and marked as the contract states. \\ * Realised profit and loss is accumulated from sales rather than recomputed from today's price, and the service is read-only on the shared trading schema. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Read the contract description block before designing anything: the definitions of cost basis, market value, and unrealised and realised profit and loss are in there and are most of the assessment. \\  \\ Build the service on its own port with its own folder, Dockerfile, compose entry and README, verifying the platform JWT and comparing the account claim against the account in the path. \\  \\ Read quantity, average cost, instrument currency and cash balance read-only, and own whatever this service owns in its own tables. \\  \\ Price with the batch quotes endpoint, up to 25 symbols per call, and cache, because a per-position loop over ten holdings costs ten times what one batched call costs for the same answer. \\  \\ Convert a multi-currency total into one base currency and handle the case where a currency cannot be converted. \\  \\ Grant the service a database role that can select from the trading tables and write only to its own. \\  \\ *Unit Test Execution Paths:* \\  \\ # positions are priced from a live quote \\ # a cached quote is reused within the cache window \\ # pricing unavailable for every symbol returns the documented service-unavailable code \\ # pricing unavailable for some symbols returns a partial answer marked as such \\ # realised profit and loss is booked at the sale and not recomputed \\ # a replayed event does not double-count realised profit and loss \\ # one account cannot read another account's portfolio \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Independent of the other three and safe to build in parallel from Monday, but start it early: it is the service most likely to be waiting on a quota, a stale quote or a currency question at four o'clock on Thursday. \\ * Stale is a state, not an error. Serve the number and mark it; hiding it and showing nothing are both worse than saying how old it is. \\ * The browser never calls Fauxnance. Prices reach the screen through this service.

Summary: End-to-End Integration on Live Data
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The chain works end to end against live data: a stored channel preference drives a trade notification, and a watchlist alert is delivered on the same channel. \\ * Each of the four services verifies the same platform token on its own, and each is reachable from the Angular application. \\ * The demonstration runs on real quotes, real messages and real rows, not fixtures. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Integrate preferences, notifications and watchlists as one chain, and integrate portfolio alongside it. \\  \\ Declare the two publish commands the harness needs so that the trade-event and market-data probes run rather than skip. \\  \\ Rotate people across the services before the last day; somebody who first opens the watchlist consumer on Friday afternoon cannot answer a question about it on Friday afternoon. \\  \\ *Integration Test* \\  \\ Set a channel preference, place a real order and confirm the notification arrives on that channel, then publish a quote that crosses a price alert and confirm the alert is delivered through notifications with no step stubbed. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Fixtures belong in the test suite. A demonstration that runs on them is demonstrating the fixture.

Summary: One Combined OWASP Security Review
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * One document, not four concatenated, covers the full OWASP Top Ten across the four services, naming the service or services each finding belongs to. \\ * Every category carries a finding and a disposition, and a category that applies to none of the four is dispositioned as out of scope with the reason rather than deleted. \\ * Findings are addressed: fixed with the commit, mitigated with what limits the exposure, or accepted with the residual risk stated. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Copy the Sprint 8 template, retitle it, name your copy in manifest.env, and write it as you build. \\  \\ Start with the access-control row, since every brief names the same first risk. \\  \\ Look by name for two risks specific to this week: a route another service calls that a customer's token can also reach, and a customer-supplied destination the service then posts to. \\  \\ Put any finding still open on Friday in the outstanding items table with an owner against it. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A category rarely lands the same way on all four services, and the row worth reading is the one that says where it landed differently. \\ * Four reviews stapled together will read as four reviews stapled together.

Summary: Architecture Decision Log
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A decision log is committed in decision-log/, one file per decision, in the shape of the provided template, with at least the number the manifest asks for. \\ * Each entry states the context, an option genuinely considered and rejected, the decision and its consequences. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Write entries as decisions are taken, not in the last hour of the sprint. \\  \\ Write an entry when reversing the choice later would cost more than an afternoon, when a competent engineer would have chosen the other option, or when somebody asked why and the answer took a paragraph. \\  \\ Favour the seams: what notifications does when preferences does not answer, how a service authenticates to a service, what happens to an alert whose delivery fails, and which service owns the customer's contact details. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * An entry with one option in it is a record of what you did. \\ * A log assembled at the end records what you built, which everyone can already see, and reads exactly like what it is.

Summary: Platform Demonstration
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The team demonstrates the running platform and the four extensions against a live stack, covering design decisions, Copilot usage and the code-quality story. \\ * Every member can walk any of the four services unaided, including the ones they did not write. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Rehearse the demonstration against the running stack rather than slides. \\  \\ Prepare to show the chain working, a replayed event producing one message rather than two, and a portfolio figure traced back to a live quote. \\  \\ Leave the repository with a green Sprint 10 harness and a local stack that starts cleanly, because the cloud week depends on both. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * This is where the platform itself is assessed for this cohort. The cloud week that follows is assessed on the deployment alone and has no panel.

Summary: Cloud Deployment (Alumni Week)
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The application is reachable over HTTPS through a CloudFront distribution, and the S3 bucket is private and returns access denied when addressed directly. \\ * Origin access control is configured, and deployment is a single script covering build, upload and invalidation. \\ * The authenticated flows are verified against the deployed front end, the deploy identity is scoped to the one bucket and the one distribution with no long-lived key in the repository, and the link is shared with the cohort. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * This week runs after Sprint 10, delivered by Fidelity as experiential learning over four and a half days with Fidelity alumni on hand. There are no Neueda instructors in the room and no live Neueda support. \\ * RUNBOOK.md in sprint-11-cloud-deploy is the instructor. Every step says what to run, what success looks like and what to do when that is not what happened. Work through it in sequence rather than mining it for commands. \\ * The alumni are there for the judgement calls the runbook cannot make. Take the steps to the runbook first. \\ * The folder is named sprint-11-cloud-deploy so that it matches the same week in every other Leap cohort; this cohort has no Sprint 11. \\ * Only the Angular application is deployed. Postgres, Kafka, the Trade REST API, the Auth service, the executor, the poller, the pipeline and the four extensions stay on Docker Compose. \\ * The AWS surface for the whole week is IAM, the AWS CLI, S3 and CloudFront. Nothing else. \\ * Assessment is asynchronous against the criteria, from what is deployed and what is committed. There is no panel this week and nothing to rehearse: the platform was demonstrated at the end of week 9. \\ * Definition of done includes sprint-11-cloud-deploy/scripts/check.sh, and scripts/check.sh --live once the deployment exists. \\ * Security focus: an origin that trusts exactly one caller, a least-privilege deploy identity, TLS enforced, and no long-lived key in any branch (OWASP A05).

Summary: Prerequisite Gate: Green Sprint 10 Harness and a Clean Local Stack
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The Sprint 10 harness passes in live mode and the local Docker Compose stack starts cleanly, both confirmed before Step 1 of the runbook. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Bring the stack up and confirm every service reports healthy. \\  \\ Run the Sprint 10 harness in live mode and fix anything red before starting the deployment, on the Monday morning if that is what it takes. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * This is a gate, not a recommendation. Every verification this week runs against the platform you already have, and debugging Sprint 10 with a distribution in front of it means you cannot tell which layer is at fault. \\ * Nothing this week stops, restarts or reconfigures a container you did not start yourself.

Summary: AWS Account, Region and the Two Identities
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * One region is chosen and used everywhere for the rest of the week. \\ * The setup identity and the deploy identity are separate, and the deploy identity is not used to create anything. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Attend the Fidelity platform SME briefing on AWS guardrails before any hands-on work; it is a briefing and not a lab, and you deploy nothing to anything belonging to Fidelity. \\  \\ Work only in the training account you are given. \\  \\ Use the region the runbook names, and use it in bucket endpoints, ARNs and CLI calls alike. \\  \\ Create the deploy user with the setup identity, once, by hand. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * CloudFront is a global edge network, so the region only decides where the bucket lives. \\ * If a call reports that your bucket must be addressed using a different endpoint, you have two regions in play, not a broken bucket.

Summary: Private S3 Bucket and the Angular Production Build
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The bucket exists, blocks all public access, and holds the Angular production build. \\ * The bucket is never addressed directly by a browser. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Create the bucket with public access blocked, and do not enable website hosting with a public read policy. \\  \\ Produce the Angular production build and upload it. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A public bucket works, and it fails this week with a working site on screen: the bucket endpoint serves over plain HTTP as well as HTTPS, everything in the bucket becomes world-readable to anyone who guesses the name, and no cache or error-page rule can sit in front of an origin being read directly.

Summary: Origin Access Control and the CloudFront Distribution
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * A CloudFront distribution fronts the bucket and serves the application over HTTPS. \\ * The bucket accepts the distribution as its only reader, and a browser resolving the bucket's own endpoint gets access denied. \\ * A public bucket policy does not satisfy this, whether or not the site loads. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Create the origin access control and make it the credential CloudFront presents when it fetches an object. \\  \\ Stand up the distribution with the S3 origin and enforce HTTPS. \\  \\ Probe both of the bucket's own endpoints and confirm they refuse, then load the distribution domain and confirm the application answers. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * Origin access control means the origin trusts exactly one caller, named and verified. A public policy means the origin trusts the internet and hopes the only thing pointing at it is your CDN. The first is a control; the second is a convention.

Summary: Scope the Deploy Identity Policy
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The deploy identity can write objects into one named bucket and create an invalidation on one named distribution, and can do nothing else. \\ * No long-lived key is present in the repository, in any branch, or in the recorded history of the sprint folder. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Start from iam/policy-skeleton.json, replace the placeholder ARNs with your own bucket name, account id and distribution id, and work the actions out from the commands you actually run. \\  \\ Include the bucket-level action a sync needs, the object-level actions an upload needs including what happens when a file present in the last build is absent from this one, and creating an invalidation plus reading its status if your script waits. \\  \\ Let an access-denied response from the CLI name the exact action it wanted rather than granting everything. \\  \\ Store the credential pair where the thing that needs it can read it and nobody else can: a named AWS CLI profile, not an export in your shell history and not a file in the repository. \\  \\ Keep the region, the bucket name and the distribution id as script arguments or environment variables rather than secrets, so the real secrets are easy to find. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A policy granting everything fails the criterion whether or not the deploy works. \\ * If the deploy credentials were pasted into a public issue tomorrow, the worst an attacker could do is replace the contents of a training front end. That containment is the point of the exercise. \\ * A key that was committed and then deleted is still a disclosed key.

Summary: One Deployment Entry Point: Build, Upload, Invalidate
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Deployment is one script covering a clean production build, the upload and the cache invalidation, in that order. \\ * Running it twice against the same commit leaves the deployment in the same state and a working site both times. \\ * Its path is declared in manifest.env. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Write the entry point so that the bucket ends up holding this build and not a mixture of this build and the last one. \\  \\ Set cache headers deliberately: the hashed assets are content-addressed and can be cached for a long time, and the entry document is the pointer to which of them are current and must never be served stale. \\  \\ Invalidate the cache, because skipping it produces the most expensive bug of the week: you deploy a fix, load the link, see the old application and debug code that is not running. \\  \\ Test the second run by running it twice and loading the site in between, not by reasoning about it.

Summary: Verify the Authenticated Flows against the Deployed Front End
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * Signing in, placing an order and watching it reach the blotter all work when driven from the CloudFront domain rather than from a development server. \\ * The API address reaches the build without becoming a value somebody edits by hand before every deploy, and the choice is written down. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Decide what the deployed build points at and get that address into the build through configuration, remembering that an address is not a secret and a key is. \\  \\ Work out what changes so that a page served from your distribution may call services that have only ever been asked by a page from the same machine, whether allowing every origin is acceptable for a service holding customer positions, and what the mixed-content rule does to an HTTPS page calling a plain HTTP API. \\  \\ Take the route the runbook gives you through both, record the decision in the decision log, and expect the assessment to read it. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * A page that renders is not a deployed application. \\ * Neither the address question nor the cross-origin question has a single right answer, and both have several wrong ones.

Summary: Share the Link, Record the Decisions and Tear Down
Description: *Acceptance Criteria:* \\  \\ * The distribution link is shared with the cohort, with one line on what works from a cold browser and one line on what needs the local stack running. \\ * The deploy entry point, the policy documents and the manifest are all committed and agree with each other. \\ * The deployment is torn down after the assessment is confirmed, and each resource is checked to be gone. \\  \\ *Tasks:* \\  \\ Post the link where everyone in the cohort can reach it. \\  \\ Write a README or decision-log entry saying what you chose and why, since nobody is in the room to ask you. \\  \\ Delete the distribution, the bucket, the origin access control and the deploy user in that order once the assessment is confirmed, and check each one is gone rather than assuming. \\  \\ *Notes:* \\  \\ * An assessor who cannot tell how the bucket became private reads it as not proven. \\ * A bucket and a distribution per team, left running, is a bill that arrives quietly for months.
